solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Country girl on booze university …

parts.note: port is a fortified wine
U is the standard abbreviation for university
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A country girl drinking at university, with the dots leading into the next clue about a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'girl on booze university' puts the girl after the drink and the college. The trailing dots only link the surface to 5 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iberian nation whose city of Oporto gave its name to the fortified wine is a sovereign state.

clue.text: Office secretaries with case for company

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant, so two of them

indicators.note: a case is the outside casing, so just the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, its outer casing

explanation.surface: Office workers carrying a briefcase for the firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' is not a workplace here but a post held, specifically that of the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: The papacy is the position and authority of the Pope, an office in the sense of a high post.

clue.text: One up around front of Argos could be a looter

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: someone up on a horse or bike is riding it

indicators.note: the front is the opening, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the shop name

explanation.surface: Someone hanging around an Argos shop might be planning to loot it.
explanation.walkthrough: Argos is a British catalogue retail chain. 'One up' means a rider, as a jockey is up on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A raider attacks a place to steal from it, which is just what a looter does during a robbery.

clue.text: Change! He couldn't out of habit!

indicators.note: a change alters the order of things, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone urged to change a habit they cannot break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' looks like a routine, but it is a monk's or nun's robe; being out of it means undressed. 'Change' also means getting changed out of clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a religious garment, so someone out of their habit has taken their clothes off and is naked.

clue.text: One aimed to shoot broadcast as full satire

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian sets out to fire off a programme of pure satire on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like a TV term, but its older sense of scattering seed makes it the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A military firearm is pointed at a target before firing, so it is a weapon aimed in order to shoot.

clue.text: … lectured for worst performance grading?

parts.note: the worst possible score is nought, shown as the letter O
a grading is the mark something is rated

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 Across, the student gets a telling-off for scoring the lowest mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Something 'rated nought' got the worst grade possible; the nought becomes the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, so someone who orated has given a lecture or address.

clue.text: Religious scholar with gas head of teaching avoided

indicators.note: something avoided is kept away from, so it is left out

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for chattering on, as to gas is; it loses its final letter

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of the word, the one removed

explanation.surface: A learned cleric talks at length but stays clear of teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gas' is a verb, idle chatter; in Britain to rabbit on is to talk endlessly. The T removed is the first letter of teaching.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish teacher and authority on religious law, so a learned figure in that faith.

clue.text: Time that bloke goes for full treatment

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the pronoun for a male person
a machine that goes is one that works

explanation.surface: The moment a man opts to have everything done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes for' looks like 'chooses', but 'goes' alone is the verb meaning functions, and 'for' is not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for everything available, as in a burger with every topping, is an idiom for the complete package.

clue.text: I'm one that hates grass turning up outside of trial

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it on both sides
in a down entry, turning upwards means reading the letters bottom to top

parts.note: a reed is a tall waterside grass
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to loathing a police informer who shows up around a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a grass is an informer, which suits the trial; here it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to loathe intensely, so the speaker is a person who feels strong hatred towards something.

clue.text: Royal papers about popular Conservative leader

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the others

parts.note: the press is the newspapers collectively
something in is fashionable or popular

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the party name

explanation.surface: The newspapers run stories about a popular leader of the Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal' looks like an adjective for the papers, but here it is a noun: a member of a royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: A daughter of a monarch is a member of the royal family, and a royal can be used as a noun for such a person.

clue.text: A tendency to ring son that's not working

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a ring encircles whatever it surrounds, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a bent is a natural inclination
S is the abbreviation for son in family trees

explanation.surface: A parent's habit of phoning a son who has no job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not working' suggests unemployment, but the answer means away from work, as an absent employee is.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker who is absent is off duty and not at the job, so they are not working that day.

clue.text: Travelling supporter?

parts.note: surface reading: a fan who follows the team to away matches
setter's reading: something that holds a person up as they move about on foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a football fan going to away games; read literally it is a prop for someone on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: A cane carried while on foot bears some of the user's weight, literally holding them up while they move.

clue.text: Description of socialism in business doctrine

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within it

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a business
red is the colour and label of socialists

explanation.surface: Defining what socialism means inside a company's guiding philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' is the traditional adjective for socialist politics, so it describes socialism.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a set of beliefs or principles, the Latin word meaning 'I believe' that opens the creed.

clue.text: USA union forced to adopt first of mandates in accord

indicators.note: something forced is pushed out of its natural shape, so the letters are rearranged
to adopt is to take in, so an extra letter joins the mix before rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An American trade union is made to take on a set of mandates it had agreed on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'USA union' reads like a trade union in America, but the two words are simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: When everyone holds the same view, with no dissent at all, a decision is unanimous and all are in agreement.

clue.text: Hairy and light-skinned part of the hand

parts.note: white describes pale skin
a knuckle is a finger joint

explanation.surface: A description of a hand: covered in hair and pale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' seems to describe a hand, but in British slang it means alarming or dangerous.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal terms for a frightening, nerve-racking experience, such as a terrifying ride that makes you grip tight.

clue.text: French article on edict poor, but not in the view of The Observer

definitions.text: not in the view of The Observer

parts.note: un is the French for a

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the letters are knocked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A piece in a French paper on a weak ruling, ignored by The Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a link meaning 'about', but it belongs to the letters being rearranged. The Observer is a British Sunday paper, here just anyone watching.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nobody watching has spotted has escaped attention, so it is not seen by an onlooker.

clue.text: Dress crab and earn capital abroad

indicators.note: to dress food is to prepare and arrange it, so the letters are set out anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Prepare seafood overseas and make money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' could be money, matching 'earn', but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Australia's seat of government is a capital city far from Britain, so a foreign seat of government.

clue.text: Bag up footwear in cloth covers?

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: a sac is a bag-like pouch
socks are worn on the feet

explanation.surface: Packing socks inside fabric covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is a term for the clergy, so 'cloth covers' are what clergy wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy wear long robes over their clothes, garments that clothe members of the ministry.

clue.text: A district, attractive and gaining recognition

parts.note: taken as written
a ward is an electoral district of a town
a winning smile is an attractive one

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood that is pretty and becoming well known.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winning' as charming, not victorious, is the less obvious sense used for the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: A product or person that collects prizes is honoured publicly, so it earns acclaim and official praise.

clue.text: Pet wearing a coat

parts.note: to pet an animal is to pat it
someone wearing a coat is in it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog dressed in a little jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an animal but is the verb, and 'coat' is a surface layer rather than a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is a thin film that forms on metal or wood with age, a surface layer like a coat of paint.

clue.text: Bosses ignoring Republican blunders

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out of account, so it is dropped

parts.note: gaffers is British slang for bosses, here without its R
R is the abbreviation for Republican, and it is dropped

explanation.surface: Leaders paying no heed to a Republican's mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a gaffer is a foreman or boss, often a football manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is an embarrassing social error or slip, so the plural is a set of clumsy mistakes.

clue.text: Couple of rounds coming from the pitcher?

definitions.text: Couple of rounds coming from the pitcher?

parts.words: Couple of rounds coming from the pitcher?
parts.note: surface reading: a jug pouring out drinks for two rounds at the bar

parts.words: Couple of rounds coming from the pitcher?
parts.note: setter's reading: round objects thrown by the pitcher in an American ball game

explanation.walkthrough: A pitcher is both a jug and the player who throws in baseball; rounds are both drinks bought for a group and spherical things.
explanation.definitionFit: In the American sport the pitcher hurls the small hard spheres towards the batter, so several of them come from that player.

clue.text: Group of beats performing for a powerful businessman

parts.note: a bar in music is a group of beats
a performer on stage is on

explanation.surface: A band playing a set for a wealthy tycoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats' suggests a drummer, but a bar is a measure of beats in written music.
explanation.definitionFit: A press or oil baron is an industry magnate, a mighty tycoon in commerce, by extension from the noble title.

clue.text: A despicable type back to pinch one half crown?

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run right to left
to pinch is to grip between fingers, so one piece is squeezed inside another

parts.note: a rat is a contemptible person
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A scoundrel returns to steal one old coin, the half-crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The half crown was an old British coin worth two shillings and sixpence; here it is a jewelled band, a partial crown, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled semicircular headpiece, rather like a crown that only goes part of the way round.

clue.text: You could say 45 minutes?
Teacher and principal picked up for naughty acts

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the words are judged by ear

parts.note: pupils call a female teacher Miss, and the principal person is the chief

explanation.surface: A teacher and head both caught misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' looks like a school head alongside the teacher, but it is the adjective meaning main.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischief is playful misbehaviour or pranks, the kind of naughtiness children get up to.

clue.text: Crimes religious types won't keep quiet

indicators.note: refusing to keep something means it is thrown out

parts.note: parsons are clergymen, here without P, the musical sign for quiet
P, piano, is the musical direction for quiet, and it is dropped

explanation.surface: Clergy committing offences they refuse to stay silent about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' looks like something the clergy won't do, but it is the letter P to be removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson is the criminal act of deliberately setting fire to property, so each such offence is a crime.

clue.text: Small child rubbishes driving proficiency sites

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a kid is a child
to pan is to criticise harshly, as a critic does

explanation.surface: A small child dismisses places for learning to drive well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbishes' is British slang for criticising scornfully, the verb sense needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: A skidpan is a slippery surface where drivers practise controlling a car that slides, improving their skill.
